title: What the Talmud is
hook: the Mishnah, gathered around 200 CE, and centuries of discussion around it, printed with commentaries on every side

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four kinds of people, and our last saying from Pirkei Avot for now. Your line was what's mine is yours. Did you give without keeping score? Today, a new part of the path. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

Picture a page unlike any other. In the middle, a small block of text. Wrapped around it, on the inside edge, a column in a different typeface. On the outside edge, another. Around those, smaller notes, cross-references, tiny letters in the margins. It looks like a city seen from the air, with an old town in the center and neighborhoods growing out in every direction. That's a page of Talmud. For the next few weeks, we'll take a taste of it. And the first surprise is that you've already been reading part of it.
screen: `A PAGE UNLIKE ANY OTHER.` → `A CITY FROM THE AIR.` → `A TASTE OF TALMUD.`

segments.voice: Start with the old town in the center. Remember Rabbi Judah the Prince, who taught that small commandments count? Around the year two hundred, he gathered generations of oral teaching into one book, the Mishnah. It's arranged in six orders, covering farming and blessings, festivals, marriage and family, damages, holy things and purity. Pirkei Avot, the sayings we've just finished, is one small tractate of it. Then the rabbis kept talking. For the next few centuries, in the academies of the land of Israel and of Babylonia, they studied every line of the Mishnah and argued over it, in Hebrew and mostly in Aramaic. That discussion is the Gemara. Put the Mishnah and the Gemara together, and you have the Talmud. There are two of them: the Jerusalem Talmud, from the land of Israel, and the larger Babylonian Talmud, which is the one most people mean. The word Talmud comes from the Hebrew root for learning and teaching. Now here's what makes it unlike most holy books. It keeps the arguments. When two sages disagree, both opinions stay on the page, often with the losing side's reasons carefully preserved. The Talmud says of the schools of Hillel and Shammai: these and these are the words of the living God. And the page keeps growing. When it was printed in Venice in the fifteen-twenties, the layout put Rashi's commentary on the inner edge and the Tosafot, later scholars from France and Germany, on the outer. Later editions added more. So a single page holds voices from many centuries, all talking at once.
screen: `THE MISHNAH: AROUND 200 CE.` · `THE GEMARA: CENTURIES OF DEBATE.` · `BOTH OPINIONS STAY ON THE PAGE.` · `RASHI INSIDE, TOSAFOT OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `A CONVERSATION ACROSS CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture the page. Settle, and breathe. Imagine the small block of text at the center: a question someone asked almost two thousand years ago. Now imagine the voices around it. A sage answering. Another disagreeing. A French commentator, Rashi, nearly nine hundred years later, writing in the margin. And at the very edge, room for you. What question would you add? After the bell, if you like, look up a picture of a Talmud page and find the center. The bell holds the time.
Talmud. Learning: the Mishnah and the centuries of discussion around it, printed with commentaries on every side.
Your line: a conversation across centuries. Today, when you disagree with someone, try to state their side so well that they'd nod, the way the Talmud keeps both. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Jews study Talmud in pairs (chavruta), reading aloud and arguing through each passage, in yeshivas, synagogues, and study groups; some learn one page every day.

options: keep it on the page, with its reasons.

notes: Review pass: the review line said yesterday (Avot 5:10) was 'the end of Pirkei Avot'; Avot continues past 5:10 (and has a sixth chapter), so it now says 'our last saying from Pirkei Avot for now'.
'Around the year 200' for the Mishnah; the Jerusalem Talmud c. 400 and the Babylonian c. 500–600 are conventional dates, left out of the voice except for the Mishnah.
Six orders glossed as farming and blessings (Zeraim, which opens with Berakhot), festivals (Moed), marriage and family (Nashim), damages (Nezikin), holy things (Kodashim), purity (Tohorot); confirm.
'These and these are the words of the living God': Eruvin 13b; paraphrased (not in quotation marks).
Daniel Bomberg's Venice edition (1520–23) fixed the pagination and the Rashi/Tosafot layout; confirm. Later editions (notably Vilna, Romm, 1880s) added more commentaries.
Pirkei Avot has no Gemara in the Babylonian Talmud; not stated in the script.
Audit (second sample): the practice put Rashi 'a thousand years' after the Mishnah (about 200 CE to about 1075); now 'nearly nine hundred years later'.
